## Mechanical and physical properties of fly ash geopolymer-mullite composites

![01973e1a-dfde-72a9-84ae-b84e3d3bb8ca_0_104_437_1375_676_0.jpg](images/01973e1a-dfde-72a9-84ae-b84e3d3bb8ca_0_104_437_1375_676_0.jpg)

# MECHANICAL AND PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF FLY ASH GEOPOLYMER - MULLITE COMPOSITES

Faisal Arif Nurgesang ${}^{1}$ , Suthee Wattanasiriwech ${}^{1}$ *, Darunee Wattanasiriwech ${}^{1}$ and Pavadee Aungkavattana ${}^{2}$

Received: July 24, 2015; Revised: September 26, 2105; Accepted: February 16, 2016

## Abstract

This work aims to investigate how compressive strength of a typical class $\mathrm{C}$ fly ash-based geopolymer would be changed with addition of mullite. In preparation of basic geopolymer, fly ash was collected from Mae Moh power plants, Lampang province, was alkaline activated and cured for a total period of 7 days. In making the composites, 20-60% of mullite powder was added to the basic geopolymer mixture and cured at the same condition. Porosity, density, and water absorption of the samples were determined by following ASTM C-642. The results showed that the compressive strength of the geopolymer mortar could be remarkably improved from 14 MPa to 71 MPa with mullite addition. The mechanical property variation of the composites was discussed along with their physical properties and microstructures.

Keywords: Geopolymer, class $\mathrm{C}$ fly ash-based geopolymer, fly ash geopolymer-mullite composites

## Introduction

In May 2015, the NOAA/Earth System Research Laboratory has announced that the level of average global atmospheric ${\mathrm{{CO}}}_{2}$ concentration reached a new high of ${401}\mathrm{{ppm}}$ (Dlugokencky and Tans, 2015). This alarmed us that we need to deal with ${\mathrm{{CO}}}_{2}$ emission more seriously. There are several sources that can contribute to ${\mathrm{{CO}}}_{2}$ emission in the world. Cement industry from all over the world generates about 7% of global ${\mathrm{{CO}}}_{2}$ emission (Davidovits,1994). Nowadays, geopolymer is a promising product that can either partially or totally replace cement (Akbari et al., 2015 and Wanjari et al., 2015). Using geopolymer helps not only reduce ${\mathrm{{CO}}}_{2}$ emission by reducing cement production, but also utilize waste material such as fly ash (Palomo et al., 1999). Fly ash is a byproduct from coal combustion process that abundant over a total of 600 metric ton per year (Joshi et al., 1997). Utilization of class $\mathrm{C}$ fly ash for making geopolymer was widely studied but commonly achieved low compressive strength (Guo et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2010; Somna et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Abdulkareem et al., 2014; Bagheri and Nazari, 2014; Abdollahnejad et al., 2015; Embong et al., 2015). Therefore, engineering class $\mathrm{C}$ fly ash based geopolymer for high compressive strength applications is a great challenge. In order to realize that, it might need to be reinforced or composited.

One of the candidates suitable for compositing with a geopolymer is mullite. Since mullite is a crystalline aluminosilicate material, it should be a highly compatible reinforcement for the geopolymer matrix system. Therefore, this study was aimed to improve the mechanical properties of fly ash based geopolymer by compositing mullite as reinforcement.

## Meterials and Methods

## Materials

Fly ash used in this study was collected from Mae Moh power plant, Lampang province, Thailand, while an industrial grade mullite powder was purchased from a local supplier in Thailand. Figure 1 presents SEM pictures of raw materials. Fly ash particle can be seen consist of spherical vitreous particles and mullite powder has irregular shape. Figure 2 presents the X-ray diffraction analysis result of raw materials. TABLE 1 presents chemical composition of fly ash and mullite as detected by X-ray Fluorescence. The chemical composition of fly ash is classified to class $\mathrm{C}$ as specified in ASTM C-168. The particle distribution of fly ash and mullite powder was measured by laser diffraction analysis (Malvern Instrument Mastersizer, 2000) as presented in TABLE 2. In this study, a mixture of chemical-grade sodium hydroxide solution and commercial sodium silicate was used as the alkaline activator.

## Sample Preparation

The optimum concentration of sodium hydroxide solution in preparation of alkaline activator was predetermined by mixing various sodium hydroxide solutions ranging from 8-16 $\mathrm{{mol}}/1$ with sodium silicate. Dry fly ash was mixed with alkaline activator and hand stirred for 1 minute. The mixture was then poured into cylindrical PVC molds ( $\varnothing {15}\mathrm{\;{mm}} \times  {30}\mathrm{\;{mm}}$ ). The geopolymer-mullite composite was prepared by adding mullite powder, ranging from 20-60 wt% of dry fly ash, to the optimized geopolymer mixture followed by the same curing procedure. The detail of various mixtures of fly ash-based geopolymer and its composites with mullite is given in TABLE 3. The samples were cured at ${90}^{ \circ  }\mathrm{C}$ for 1 day and then at ${40}^{ \circ  }\mathrm{C}$ for 6 days.

## Setting Time and Compressive Strength

The setting time of geopolymer paste was tested according to ASTM C-191 with a manually operated standard Vicat apparatus. The compressive strength was measured after 7 days of curing. The samples were demolded from cylindrical PVC molds, and subjected to the compressive test by using Universal Testing Machine (Instron 5566) with the loading speed of $1\mathrm{\;{mm}}/\mathrm{{min}}$ . Each reported value is the average of five samples.

## Scanning Electron Microscopy

A scanning microscopy was used to analyze the morphology of polishing surfaces. All samples were polished with SiC grinding paper number P600 for $1\mathrm{\;{min}}$ with a rotational speed of ${180}\mathrm{{rpm}}$ and then on number P1200 for ${30}\mathrm{{sec}}$ with a rotational speed of ${200}\mathrm{{rpm}}$ . Finally, the samples were polished using ${6\mu }\mathrm{m}$ diamond particles. All the samples were gold coated prior to SEM observation.

## Density, Voids, and Apparent Density Measurement

Determination of porosity, density, and water absorption of geopolymer was performed by following ASTM C-642. The average values were obtained from five samples.

## Results and Discussion

## Effect of NaOH Concentration

The compressive strength of fly ash-based geopolymers activated by various sodium hydroxide-sodium silicate solutions are given in Figure 3. The compressive strength is increasing with the increase of sodium hydroxide concentration. The significant improvement starts at ${10}\mathrm{\;{mol}}/\mathrm{l}$ and the compressive strength does not increase significantly after ${12}\mathrm{\;{mol}}/\mathrm{l}$ . In this condition, small error bar indicates that the compressive strength result was consistent. However, at 16 mol/l the compressive strength was still a high value, but the strength result was inconsistent. Therefore, the optimum sodium hydroxide concentration at ${12}\mathrm{\;{mol}}/\mathrm{l}$ was chosen. This result was also in good agreement with previous work (Al Bakri et al., 2012 and Arioz et al., 2012).

## Effect of Mullite Addition

The compressive strength of ${20} - {60}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ mullite added geopolymer composite is given in Figure 4. It showed that by adding just ${20}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ of mullite the compressive strength of the geopolymer was increased significantly to ${44}\mathrm{{MPa}}$ , i.e. three times stronger than the fly ash-geopolymer without addition. By adding ${40}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ of mullite, a remarkable improvement in compressive strength, ${71}\mathrm{{MPa}}$ , was achieved. However, at 60 wt% of mullite addition, the compressive strength decreased to ${58}\mathrm{{MPa}}$ . It can be concluded that ${40}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ is the optimum level of mullite addition into fly ash-based geopolymer. microstructures, as shown in Figure 8. Ina composite with 20 wt% addition, small mullite crystals could be observed within the matrix of geopolymer, associated with an improvement in compressive strength. At ${40}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ addition, more mullite crystals with longer and larger needle-like shape were detected. Small needlelike structure and interlocking of mullite crystals were proposed to be the key factor for achieving high strength (Carty and Senapati, 1998). With its high aspect ratio, mullite crystal could effectively help resist crack propagation and successfully reinforce the matrix in composite system. As a result, the compressive strength was the highest with such microstructure. However, even though the mullite crystal was found overa broader area in the case of ${60}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ addition, but compressive strength in this condition was not as high as at ${40}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ . It could be because the ratio of solid to liquid has become too low, so the activator was insufficient to dissolve the raw materials, indicated by the presence of unreacted fly ash particles under SEM observation.

Fly ash-based geopolymer has lower bulk and apparent density, and relatively high volume of permeable voids at 24.9%. This existing voids tend to absorbs more water. In contrast, fly ash geopolymer -mullite composite has higher bulk and apparent density, low volume of permeable voids, and low water absorption. At low concentration of $8 - {10}\mathrm{\;{mol}}/\mathrm{l}$ , the $\mathrm{{NaOH}}$ solution could not effectively dissolve fly ash particles. However, when the concentration was increased to ${12}\mathrm{{mol}}/\mathrm{l}$ , the fly ash was successfully dissolved, resulting in an average compressive strength with great consistency of 14 MPa. The addition of mullite into fly ash-based geopolymer could increase the compressive strength significantly i.e., specimen with 40 wt% of mullite addition reached an average of ${71}\mathrm{{MPa}}$ . ## Abstract

The main objective of this study was to apply geopolymer (GP) particles as novelty fillers in natural rubber (NR) composites with various loadings $(0,{10},{20},{30}$ , and 40 phr). Influence of GP particles on cure characteristics, mechanical, dynamic, thermal, and morphological properties of the NR/geopolymer composites was investigated. It was found that incorporation of geopolymer particles significantly affected the cure characteristics and the mechanical properties. That is, faster curing was observed due to acceleration by metal oxide impurities. It was also found that ${100}\%$ modulus and tensile strength increased with the addition of ${10}\mathrm{{phr}}\mathrm{{GP}}$ . This is attributed to the physical interactions of GP particles with NR molecules. In addition, the Payne effect and improved thermal stability were also observed in the GP-filled NR composites. It was concluded that ${10}\mathrm{{phr}}$ of GP in NR composites might be suitable for some industrial applications.

## KEYWORDS

composites, geopolymer, mechanical properties, natural rubber, thermal properties

## 1 INTRODUCTION

Polymer composites combine a polymer matrix with fillers. They are attractive in industrial applications and for academic research, due to control of the material properties. Natural rubber (NR) as a green and renewable polymer is widely used as a raw polymer material industrially, including in automotive parts and tires, because of its excellent mechanical and elastic properties. ${}^{\left\lbrack  1\right\rbrack  }$ However, fillers are necessary in most cases to modify the NR properties for specific applications. A wide variety of particulate fillers are used in the rubber industry for multiple purposes, including reinforcement, reduced material costs, and improved processing. ${}^{\left\lbrack  2\right\rbrack  }$ The most important fillers in rubber compounding are the conventional synthetic fillers based on carbon black and silica. They reinforce and enhance various properties such as tear strength, tensile strength, hardness, and abrasion resistance. ${}^{\left\lbrack  3\right\rbrack  }$ The incorporation of solid particles with large specific surface, such as synthetic silica, quartz, carbonaceous materials, and metal oxides, provided ample filler surface to interact with the rubber molecules, and hence these are very effective in improving rubber properties. ${}^{\left\lbrack  4\right\rbrack  }$ Synthetic silicas, for instance precipitated silica, possess siloxane and acidic silanol groups (Si-OH), ${}^{\left\lbrack  5\right\rbrack  }$ and have also been widely used in the polymer industries. ${}^{\left\lbrack  6\right\rbrack  }$ Typically the silica surfaces are hydrophilic, so they have strong tendency to adsorb moisture. ${}^{\left\lbrack  7\right\rbrack  }$ Furthermore, when large amounts of silica are added, the compound viscosity is increased substantially due to strong silica-silica interactions, ${}^{\left\lbrack  8\right\rbrack  }$ and the production of these conventional fillers is highly energy-consuming. Thus, alternative fillers from renewable resources are of considerable interest to improve the properties of rubber while improving sustainability and green aspects of the rubber life cycle.

In recent years, silica from natural sources has attracted attention as an alternative reinforcing filler in natural and synthetic rubber, because of low cost, good mechanical properties, dimensional stability, and environmental issues. ${}^{\left\lbrack  9\right\rbrack  }$ Types of natural fillers exploited in rubber composites include fly ash (FA), ${}^{\left\lbrack  {10}\right\rbrack  }$ rice husk ash (RHA), ${}^{\left\lbrack  {11}\right\rbrack  }$ oil palm ash (OPA), ${}^{\left\lbrack  {12}\right\rbrack  }$ bagasse fiber ash (BFA), ${}^{\left\lbrack  {13}\right\rbrack  }$ cellulose fiber, ${}^{\left\lbrack  {14}\right\rbrack  }$ coconut shell powder (CSP), ${}^{\left\lbrack  {15}\right\rbrack  }$ and lignin. ${}^{\left\lbrack  {16}\right\rbrack  }$ The FA is a byproduct from the combustion of pulverized coal in electric power generating plants. It is a potential alternative filler in rubber materials with nearly ${40} - {50}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ silica content. ${}^{\left\lbrack  {10}\right\rbrack  }$ In addition, FA contains various chemical elements, including aluminum, iron, calcium, magnesium, sulfur, sodium, potassium, and carbon. On the other hand, RHA filler has also been tested in natural rubber compounds. ${

In addition, OPA filler was also used in rubber compounds, and tensile strength and elongation at break improved by about ${16}\%$ and ${7.4}\%$ , respectively. ${}^{\left\lbrack {18}\right\rbrack }$ ![01974484-c8d5-72ac-a6d1-acf6a850ed04_1_126_130_1011_755_0.jpg](images/01974484-c8d5-72ac-a6d1-acf6a850ed04_1_126_130_1011_755_0.jpg) FIGURE 1 Geopolymerization reactions of fly ash with alkaline solution. $\mathrm{M} +$ refers to alkali cations Geopolymers (GPs) are polymerized chains or networks of inorganic aluminosilicate molecules linked with covalent bonds. ${}^{\left\lbrack {19}\right\rbrack }$ They are synthesized at room temperature from predominantly silica and aluminum materials of geological origin, or with by-products such as fly ash, as geopolymer-ization process shown in Figure 1. The geopolymers are a comparatively new type of material containing pozzolan components and alkaline solution. It is noted that fly ash has been frequently used as the pozzolan material in the synthesis of GPs. ${}^{\left\lbrack {20}\right\rbrack }$ Therefore, geopolymers can be produced from waste materials and thus reduce environmental problems. In particular, a new and green solution is to utilize fly ash to avoid its negative impacts on environment and ecology, instead trapping the toxic trace metal elements in geopolymer structures. ${}^{\left\lbrack {21}\right\rbrack }$ The fly ash-based geopolymers typically exhibit superior mechanical properties with low density and cage-like crystalline structure. ${}^{\left\lbrack {19}\right\rbrack }$ Furthermore, their durability has been recognized as nearly comparable to that of hydrated Portland cement, and they can be used as green cement. ${}^{\left\lbrack {22}\right\rbrack }$ Geopolymers might also have use as new alternative fillers that improve various properties of rubber composites. This is because geopolymers contain Si and Al ions that could form linkages with organic polymer molecules. Therefore, the geopolymer might interact with the rubber molecules, which enhances reinforcement effects. These might be innovative and advantageous fillers in natural rubber composites. Therefore, the novel NR/GP composites which were prepared in this work had benefit over the conventional fillers in particular low energy-consuming process. In this work, novel geopolymer-filled NR composites were prepared with various geopolymer contents. The main objective was to determine the effects of geopolymer on the properties of NR composites. In addition, fly ash was also compounded with NR for comparison purposes. ### 2.2 | Preparation of geopolymers Fly ash was first mixed with ${10}\mathrm{M}\mathrm{{NaOH}}$ solution in a Hobart mixer for about $2\mathrm{\;{min}}$ , with a paddle speed of approximately ${285}\mathrm{{rpm}}$ . Then, the ${\mathrm{{Na}}}_{2}{\mathrm{{SiO}}}_{3}$ solution was added, and mixing was continued for another 2 min. The mixture was then immediately cast into a mold and conditioned at room temperature for at least $4\mathrm{\;{hr}}$ as the final setting time. It was then annealed by conditioning in a hot air oven at approximately ${65}^{ \circ }\mathrm{C}$ for $4\mathrm{{hr}}$ and then further annealed in a microwave at ${450}\mathrm{\;W}$ for $5\mathrm{\;{min}}$ . Finally, the geopolymer product was ground in a ball mill for about ${48}\mathrm{{hr}}$ . Then, the geopolymer powder was sieved through a 200-mesh screen before compounding with NR. The functional groups in the geopolymer particles were characterized by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Vertex70, Bruker, Karlsruhe, Germany). Also, the particle size distribution of geopolymer was analyzed by a particle size analyzer (Beckman Coulter LS 230, Vernon Hills, IL, USA). The morphology of geopolymer particles was also imaged by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI-Quanta 400, Jeol Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). Each powder was first dried to constant weight in a hot air oven at about ${100}^{ \circ }\mathrm{C}$ over 14 hr. The sample was then treated in a muffle furnace by heating from 50 to $1,{000}^{ \circ }\mathrm{C}$ . It was then mixed with a binder (i.e., WAX C) in the weight ratio 2:1 and then compressed to a thin sheet. Finally, the sheet samples were characterized by XRF. ### 2.4 | Preparation of NR/geopolymer composites Natural rubber/geopolymer composites were prepared by dry mixing at room temperature using a two-roll mill. It can be seen that the alkali facilitated decomposition of aluminosilicate in the fly ash and then favored polycondensation. The reaction proceeds under mild temperatures in the range from 25 to ${90}^{ \circ }\mathrm{C}$ , so it is considered energy efficient and practical. Apparently, the reactions between fly ash and alkali and condensation of the resultant ${\mathrm{{Si}}}^{4 + }$ and ${\mathrm{{Al}}}^{3 + }$ species took place, followed by nucleation, oligomerization, and polymerization. This finally led to new aluminosilicate-based polymers with amorphous three-dimensional geopolymer networks. The fly ash-based geopolymer paste was cast into a mold at room temperature to settle in its final form. The alkali activation of fly ash is critical to geopolymerization. It is known that the alkaline solutions (i.e., ${\mathrm{{Na}}}_{2}{\mathrm{{SiO}}}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{{NaOH}}$ ), silica, alumina, and aluminosilicate in fly ash, are important factors controlling geopolymerization and structure of the final geopolymer. ${}^{\left\lbrack {27}\right\rbrack }$ Upon hydrolysis, the -Si-O-Si- or -Si-O-Al- bonds in aluminosilicate were broken, and the active ${\mathrm{{Al}}}^{3 + }$ and ${\mathrm{{Si}}}^{4 + }$ species were released. These active species shared electrons with the $4{\mathrm{O}}^{2 - }$ ions to form nuclei and aluminosilicate oligomers of tetrahedral ${\mathrm{{SiO}}}_{4}$ and ${\mathrm{{AlO}}}_{4}$ . Then, the aluminosilicate oligomers could be linked to form polysialate with -Al-O-Si- chains, polysialate siloxo -Al-O-Si-Si- chains, and polysialate disiloxo -Al-O-Si-Si-Si-chains. ${}^{\left\lbrack {28}\right\rbrack }$ The geopolymer formed here consisted of ${30}\mathrm{{wt}}\%$ ${\mathrm{{SiO}}}_{2},{17.9}\mathrm{{wt}}\% \mathrm{{CaO}},{12.4}\mathrm{{wt}}\% {\mathrm{{Al}}}_{2}{\mathrm{O}}_{3}$ , and other substances (Table 4). ![01974484-c8d5-72ac-a6d1-acf6a850ed04_4_636_1723_1005_472_0.jpg](images/01974484-c8d5-72ac-a6d1-acf6a850ed04_4_636_1723_1005_472_0.jpg) FIGURE 3 Scanning electron microscopy micrographs of (a) geopolymer and (b) fly ash particles

It is seen that the NR composites with 10 or ${20}\mathrm{{phr}}\mathrm{{GP}}$ exhibited higher Young’s and ${100}\%$ moduli (i.e., final positions in the graph insert) and stress-strain curves raised above that of the gum vulcanizate. However, incorporating more than 20 phr GP (or 10 phr FA) gave similar stress-strain curves to the gum vulcanizate but with different failure location or elongation at break. The geopolymer at 10 or ${20}\mathrm{{phr}}$ reduced the mobility of molecular chains and hence increased stiffness of the material. In contrast, incorporating 30 or 40 phr GP (or 10 phr FA) lowered the ${100}\%$ modulus and the stress-strain curve from those of the gum NR vulcanizate. It can be seen that the GP/NR (10 phr) vulcanizate exhibited higher tensile strength but lower elongation at break than the gum NR vulcanizate. This may be due to the interactions of geopolymer and NR that improved the strength but reduced the ability to extend. Generally, the absolute value of ${\mathrm{G}}^{\prime }$ in the low-strain regime relates to filler-filler networks. It is seen that ${\mathrm{G}}^{\prime }$ in the low-strain regime for the GP-filled NR composites increased with filler loading, while the FA-filled NR composite had the lowest value. This implies that the filler-filler networks grew with geopolymer loading while the FA filler networks were weaker. It is noted that the network formation by a filler in NR matrix is strongly related to the specific surface area and the self-aggregation tendency. That is, the FA with lower specific surface than the GP had less interfacial filler-filler interactions. ## 4 | CONCLUSIONS

Geopolymer (GP) was successfully used as an alternative novelty filler in NR composite vulcanizates. It was found that the GP-filled NR composites had faster scorch and cure times, and higher cure rate index than the gum NR vulcanizate. Furthermore, the NR composites with 10 phr GP exhibited higher ${100}\%$ modulus and tensile strength than the NR/FA composite with similar level of fly ash (FA) loading, due to the stronger interactions of GP and NR matrix and the better GP filler distribution with smaller aggregates. Furthermore, larger cavities or voids were observed in the composites with high GP contents (i.e., 30 and 40 phr), as excessive filler loading caused large agglomerates and cavities in the composites because the adhesion of NR and GP was not sufficiently strong. In addition, the NR composite with 10 phr GP exhibited finer and better dispersion of the particles in the NR matrix than seen in the NR/FA composite. It was also found that in the low-strain regime, the storage modulus ${\mathrm{G}}^{\prime }$ of NR composites increased with GP filler loading, while the FA-filled NR composite had the lowest value. This relates to the Payne effect and filler-filler interactions in the composites. In addition, the thermal stability of GP-filled NR composites was slightly improved from that of the gum NR. Therefore, it is concluded that that ${10}\mathrm{{phr}}$ of GP in NR composites might be suitable for some industrial applications.
